concept: A usable estimate of almost any quantity comes from decomposing it into independently guessable factors, multiplying them while tracking units, and aiming for the right order of magnitude rather than a precise figure.
across: Space & Astronomy — Frank Drake's 1961 equation for the number of communicating galactic civilizations is the same Fermi-chain method, and also shows where it breaks: several of its factors are uncertain by many orders of magnitude, not just a factor of a few.
claim: A disciplined chain of rough, independently-guessable factors can land within a factor of two of ground truth even with no instruments at all (Fermi at Trinity, 10,000 tons guessed vs. a measured yield of 18.6-24.8 kt) — but the same method, applied to the Drake equation, shows that when individual factors are uncertain by many orders of magnitude rather than a factor of a few, the chain stops producing a trustworthy number at all. Decomposition is not by itself a guarantee of accuracy; it only works as well as its least-certain link.
label: settled
evidence: Fermi's 1945 Trinity memo; J. I. Katz, "Fermi at Trinity" (Nuclear Technology, 2021); H. D. Selby et al., 2021 Trinity yield reassessment; Drake equation history checked via web search (Green Bank, Nov. 1961).

concept: Constant-percentage growth compounds, and a logarithmic scale turns that compounding into a straight line whose slope is the growth rate.
across: AI — OpenAI's 2018 'AI and Compute' analysis found training compute for the largest AI runs grew ~300,000-fold from 2012-2018, doubling roughly every 3.4 months, read with the same straight-line-on-a-log-plot method Moore used on transistor counts.
claim: A trend line fitted to past compounding data describes the rate that held in the past, not a law bound to continue — Moore's own 1975 revision of his 1965 forecast is the method's inventor making that correction in public, and it is a recurring failure mode whenever people extrapolate a 'law' from a short run of real data.
label: settled
evidence: Gordon Moore, 'Cramming more components onto integrated circuits' (Electronics, 1965) and his 1975 IEEE paper revising the doubling period, both checked via web search against the Computer History Museum's and IEEE's own accounts this run.

concept: Scale an object up with its shape fixed and area grows as the square of its size while volume and weight grow as the cube, so any property depending on their ratio changes with size.
across: Engineering — Galileo's Two New Sciences (1638) used the same square-cube argument to show a scaled-up wooden beam collapses under its own weight, which is why structural design is never just a bigger photograph of a smaller design.
claim: The square-cube law is settled geometry, but Kleiber's widely used 3/4-power rule for metabolic rate is not: West, Brown and Enquist's 1997 theoretical derivation from branching supply networks and White and Seymour's 2003 empirical re-analysis of 619 mammal species (finding closer to 2/3) still disagree, nearly a century after Kleiber's original 1932 study, on both the exact exponent and why it holds — a reminder that a number everyone uses is not automatically a number everyone has agreed on.
label: debated
evidence: J. B. S. Haldane, "On Being the Right Size" (Harper's Magazine, 1926); Max Kleiber (1932); West, Brown & Enquist, Science 276 (1997); White & Seymour, PNAS (2003); Galileo, Two New Sciences (1638). All checked via web search this run.
